extraction_text: Suka approached his father Vyasa, seeking knowledge of liberation (moksha).
Vyasa instructed Suka to learn the scriptures of liberation and all dharmas.

attributes.relationship: Teacher and student, father and son

extraction_text: Suka mastered the Yoga Sutras and the teachings of Kapila under Vyasa's guidance.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Possesses power like Brahma, aided by the goddess of speech

extraction_text: Vyasa directed Suka to go to King Janaka of Mithila for further instruction on liberation.
Vyasa gave Suka specific instructions: travel by foot (not by air), follow the proper path without seeking shortcuts, and obey Janaka humbly.

attributes.significance: Emphasis on humility and proper conduct despite Suka's supernatural abilities

extraction_text: Suka journeyed on foot from his homeland to Mithila, passing through various lands and natural obstacles.

attributes.route: Crossed mountains, rivers, lakes, forests; passed through Meru, Hari, and Himavat countries, reached Bharata; saw regions of Chinese and Huns, reached Aryavarta

extraction_text: Suka remained focused on his mission, ignoring distractions like beautiful cities, gardens, and jewels along the way.
Suka arrived in the prosperous kingdom of Videha, protected by King Janaka, and reached the city of Mithila.

attributes.description: Land abundant with villages, food, cattle, grains, birds, and lotuses

extraction_text: Suka entered Mithila, proceeded to the royal palace, and was stopped by guards at the gate and palace entrance.

attributes.challenge: Faced obstruction from guards but remained patient and unangered

extraction_text: Suka waited patiently at the palace entrance, enduring physical hardships from the journey without showing fatigue.

attributes.significance: Shows humility and readiness to receive teaching from King Janaka

extraction_text: A compassionate gatekeeper saw Sukha standing like the midday sun, paid homage to him with folded hands, and allowed him to enter the second wall of the royal palace.
Sukha sat there contemplating liberation, treating shade and sunlight equally.

supernatural_elements: Equal treatment of shade and sunlight (spiritual detachment)

extraction_text: The king's minister arrived, paid homage with folded hands, and allowed Sukha to enter the third wall of the royal palace.
The minister guided Sukha into the beautiful garden connecting to the harem, seated him appropriately, and departed.
Over fifty beautiful young women, skilled in flirtation, music, and dance, approached Sukha, showed him highest respect, offered foot-washing water and delicious food.
After Sukha ate, the women showed him the beautiful harem gardens while playing, laughing, and singing.
Sukha, born from firewood, remained pure-souled, controlled his senses, suppressed anger, and showed neither happiness nor anger.
The women prepared a magnificent jewel-encrusted bed for Sukha.
Sukha washed his feet, recited evening prayers, sat on a clean cushion, and contemplated liberation.
Sukha spent the first watch of night in deep contemplation, slept during the middle watch according to rules, woke up, purified himself, and resumed contemplation surrounded by the women.
King Janaka, accompanied by ministers, priests, and harem attendants, approached Sukha bearing cushions, jewels, and food.

relationships: King Janaka shows respect to Sukha

extraction_text: King Janaka received a jewel-encrusted cushion from the priest and respectfully presented it to Sukha.
After Sukha sat down, King Janaka paid homage according to scriptures, offering foot-washing water, food, and a cow, which Sukha accepted with proper etiquette.

relationships: Mutual respect between king and sage

extraction_text: Sukha accepted King Janaka's offerings and the cow, greeted the king, and wished him and his entourage prosperity, happiness, and good health.
With Sukha's permission, the noble-hearted King Janaka sat on the ground with folded hands along with his entourage.
King Janaka greeted Sukha, son of Vyasa, and asked about the purpose of his visit.
Sukha explained that he came on his father Vyasa's instruction to seek Janaka's teachings about Brahmin duties and liberation.
King Janaka described the traditional four stages of a Brahmin's life: student, householder, forest-dweller, and renunciant.
Sukha questioned whether someone who already understands eternal knowledge still needs to follow the four life stages.
King Janaka explained that liberation requires both knowledge and a teacher, but ultimately both are transcended.

supernatural_elements: Metaphor of teacher as helmsman, knowledge as boat

extraction_text: King Janaka described the path to liberation through seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self.
King Janaka quoted verses previously recited by King Yayati about the nature of liberation.
The text describes the qualities of one who attains Brahman (the ultimate reality).

attributes.description: Describes equanimity towards opposites (praise/blame, gold/iron, pleasure/pain, cold/heat, gain/loss, love/hate, life/death) and control of senses as qualities leading to Brahman.

extraction_text: A speaker addresses a learned Brahmin, acknowledging his qualities and knowledge.

attributes.description: The speaker states the Brahmin possesses the described qualities, has transcended sensory objects through his teacher's grace and learning, and is on the path to liberation, but may not fully realize his own state due to youth, doubt, or fear.

extraction_text: The speaker offers guidance to resolve doubts and achieve liberation.

attributes.description: The speaker suggests that sincere devotion and resolving doubts with the help of someone like himself can untie knots and achieve the goal. He reaffirms the Brahmin's attainment, equanimity, and freedom from desire and fear.

extraction_text: The speaker concludes by stating the Brahmin is already established in the fruit of Brahminhood and liberation.

attributes.description: The speaker asserts the Brahmin is on the supreme, indestructible path, embodying the nature of liberation, and questions what more he needs to ask.

extraction_text: The text is identified as a passage from the Mahabharata.

attributes.description: The passage is cited as Chapter 313 of the Shanti Parva (Book of Peace) of the Mahabharata.
